items.title: Tell someone your plans
items.text:
Before you leave, give a responsible person your route, who is travelling, your vehicle, and when you expect to arrive or return. Agree a time to check in. When you arrive safely, tell them.
- Include who is with you and when you expect to be back. If you do not return on time, your contact can raise the alarm with police (NSW National Parks).
- For longer trips or remote areas, NSW National Parks highly recommends filling in a trip intention form and taking a personal locator beacon (PLB).
- Arrange scheduled contact, and an emergency plan if you do not reach a place by the agreed time. Allow for minor delays (South Australia).
- If you plan to leave a main road, tell someone you trust your intended route and expected arrival time, and let them know you have arrived (Northern Territory).

items.title: Plan your route and check conditions
items.text:
Good planning prevents most outback problems. Check conditions before you leave, and again along the way.
- Use maps to prepare your itinerary and take them with you. Carry detailed paper maps: GPS and other navigation devices are good but may stop working in some conditions (Queensland Parks).
- Do not make your schedule too tight. Allow for unexpected delays.
- Check the weather forecast, park alerts or closures, and road conditions before you go.
- Unsealed roads may be impassable after rain, and many outback roads are unsuitable for 2WD vehicles.
- Check where the nearest food and fuel are before you go.
- Know who manages the road. In South Australia, severe penalties apply for driving on closed roads and they are enforced.
- During the Northern Territory wet season some roads and tracks can become impassable. Check the NT road report before heading off.

items.title: Best time to travel: heat, cold and the wet season
items.text:
Outback weather can be extreme. Choose your season and your daily plan with that in mind.
- Outback NSW can reach up to 50 degrees Celsius in some places in summer. Nights can be cold and temperatures can drop well below 0 degrees Celsius at times in winter. Autumn and spring are the best times for extended stays and long drives (NSW National Parks).
- The Royal Flying Doctor Service advises against travelling in the hottest part of the year.
- Extreme cold in the southern Northern Territory can be just as dangerous as heat in the north (NT Emergency Service).
- In the Northern Territory some roads and tracks may be impassable in the wet season, which the NT Emergency Service gives as November to April. Other agencies may give different months, so check locally before you go.

items.title: Plan your fuel stops
items.text:
Fuel use varies a lot on remote tracks, so plan every leg.
- Carry enough fuel between all stops. Soft sand, muddy tracks and slow hilly terrain all increase fuel use (South Australia).
- The lighter you travel, the lower your fuel use and the less wear on your vehicle (South Australia).
- Calculate driving distances, check refuelling points and allow plenty of travelling time (Queensland Parks).
- Check where fuel and food are available before you go. For remote trips, consider carrying extra fuel in a suitable fuel container, plus spare tyres and wheel-changing equipment (NSW National Parks).
- Towing a caravan: fuel use rises for most light vehicles, particularly at speeds over 90 km/h, so plan to refuel more often (Transport for NSW).

items.title: What to pack for remote driving
items.text:
NSW National Parks and Queensland Transport both list these basics. They say the list is not extensive, so add to it for your trip.
- First aid kit, including a snake bite kit.
- Water: 20 litres for emergency use, plus 4 litres per person per day. See the water guide for other agencies' figures.
- Communication equipment. Your mobile phone may not work in the outback.
- Food for all days of the trip, plus extra to cover delays.
- Fire extinguisher.
- Tool kit suited to the vehicle and trailer, including tyre-changing equipment. Queensland lists a jack, winder, wheel brace, spanners, screwdrivers, a spare fan belt, hoses and fuses.
- Two spare wheels (NSW says you may need 2, depending on the trip).
- Shovel in case you get bogged, and recovery equipment if you plan to go off-road.
- Compass or GPS, and maps.
- Tarpaulin or other shade, and a blanket.
- Cooler or fridge, rubbish bags, toilet paper, matches or a lighter.
- Hat, sunscreen and insect repellent.

items.title: Medical readiness for remote travel
items.text:
The Royal Flying Doctor Service says up to a quarter of the emergency medical evacuations it carries out each year are city travellers who get into trouble on an outback trip. It also says there are four times more injuries in remote areas than in towns and cities.
- Carry a summary of your medical history, all your medication and repeat scripts.
- Do a first aid course and pack a first aid kit.
- Take a hat, sunscreen and insect repellent, and clothing suited to the climate. Take warmer clothes for the evenings.
- Overseas visitors are encouraged to take out adequate travel insurance when travelling in outback Australia.
- Dial 000 for emergency services and be prepared to give your location.

items.title: Driver fatigue: breaks and daily limits
items.text:
Distances are long and fatigue is one of the most frequent causes of serious crashes in the Northern Territory.
- Take a break every 2 hours and do not drive for more than 8 to 10 hours a day. Plan the rest areas and driver reviver sites you will use (Queensland).
- Do not drive when you are tired. Towing is more tiring than normal driving, so plan fewer hours on the road each day and more rest breaks (Transport for NSW).
- Heat adds to fatigue and dehydration, which slow reaction times (RACV). Drink water and take regular breaks.

items.title: Mobile coverage in remote Australia
items.text:
Mobile coverage is limited outside towns and main roads. Plan to be out of range.
- South Australia says only about five per cent of the outback has mobile phone range, with most coverage in townships on main sealed roads. Coverage is sporadic on the unsealed road network.
- NSW National Parks warns your mobile phone may not work in the outback.
- Take other ways to call for help: a satellite phone, a UHF radio and a personal locator beacon (PLB). Carry a list of local UHF channels and emergency contacts (Queensland Parks).
- Tell someone your route and when to expect you. See the guide on telling someone your plans.

items.title: Emergency+ app and giving your location
items.text:
Emergency+ is a free app developed by Australia's emergency services and their government and industry partners. It helps you contact emergency services and shows your location.
- Download it before you leave. It only works with mobile reception, so it cannot replace a satellite phone or beacon (NSW National Parks).
- The Royal Flying Doctor Service says the app shows your longitude and latitude and helps emergency services find you. It may work in some areas that have data coverage but no mobile voice coverage.
- It can be switched off when not needed, to save battery (Royal Flying Doctor Service).
- If you do not have a smartphone, watch for crossroads as you travel and mark your journey on a map, so you can describe where you are.
- Call 000 for emergencies and be ready to say where you are.

items.title: UHF CB radio channels
items.text:
UHF CB radio is widely used in the outback. These are the channel uses given by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) and South Australia's Landscape Board. Check the current rules before you travel.
- Channels 5 and 35 are for emergency messages only. Volunteers monitor them and they may not always be available in outback regions. Fines and imprisonment can apply for misuse (South Australia).
- Channel 40 is the road or truckies channel (South Australia).
- Channels 9 to 30, 39 and 49 to 70 can be used for conversations. Anyone within range (line of sight) can hear you.
- Channels 1 to 8 and 41 to 48 are repeater channels that carry up to about 100 km. Use them only to seek assistance (South Australia). ACMA says if there is no repeater nearby they can be used on a single frequency, but this can interfere with a repeater a long way away.
- Channels 31 to 38 and 71 to 78 are repeater inputs. Do not use them for ordinary conversations.
- Channels 22 and 23 are for data only. You cannot speak on them.
- Emergency channel 9 (27.065 MHz) is for emergency messages in the HF CB band (ACMA).

items.title: Satellite phones and HF radio
items.text:
Mobile coverage runs out. Satellite and HF options can reach almost anywhere.
- Satellite telephones provide communications to almost anywhere in Australia. Some outback locations, such as Birdsville and Mt Dare, hire satellite phones to travellers (South Australia).
- High Frequency (HF) radio can give reliable communications over thousands of kilometres. South Australia says it offers no-cost communications between mobiles travelling anywhere in Australia and with base stations of the VKS-737 radio network.
- The Royal Flying Doctor Service suggests a satellite phone is a good idea for travel to a remote area.
- Queensland Parks recommends reliable communication equipment such as a satellite phone or UHF radio, with a list of local UHF channels and emergency contacts.

items.title: Personal locator beacons (PLBs)
items.text:
A PLB is an electronic distress beacon. It helps rescuers find your position when you cannot call for help.
- Only activate a PLB when you are in danger or injured (Queensland Parks).
- South Australia says PLBs can be activated in life-threatening situations and must be registered with the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA).
- NSW National Parks highly recommends taking a PLB for longer trips or remote areas, along with a trip intention form.

items.title: How much water to carry
items.text:
Agencies give different figures because regions, seasons and trip types differ. These are the figures from each source. Check with the land manager or local visitor centre for your route and season.
- NSW National Parks and Queensland Transport: 20 litres for emergency use, plus 4 litres per person per day.
- South Australia (outback): carry adequate water plus a reserve for three to four days. Estimate 6 litres per person per day in mild weather and 10 litres per person per day in warmer weather.
- Northern Territory Emergency Service: drink at least 2 litres a day, and more if outdoors or exercising. Carry plenty of water, at least 20 litres.
- Royal Flying Doctor Service: store water in small containers rather than one large tank, and check every container for leaks. Most towns have water, but at some places you may not be able to get drinking water.
- Do not rely on waterholes, dams, bores, mills, tanks or troughs.
- Hot and tropical regions (central and northern Australia): NT Government park advice for the Red Centre and the Top End is to drink water regularly even in milder temperatures, and to drink at least 1 litre of water per hour when outside. Central Australia has extreme heat from November to March. The Top End can be hot and humid from October to March (NT Government, Stay safe in the heat in parks).
- Needs rise in summer, in extremely hot climates and with hard exertion: the NHMRC says adults living or working in extremely hot climates may need more than its standard fluid intakes to stay hydrated, especially if they are very active. It also says that in summer, when heat stress may be high, water depletion can lead to heat exhaustion, loss of consciousness and heat stroke (NHMRC, Eat for Health). This is why the figures above should be treated as a starting point, not a limit.

items.title: Dehydration: signs and prevention
items.text:
Dehydration happens when you do not have enough fluid in your body. Severe dehydration can be life threatening, especially for babies, young children and older people (healthdirect).
- Mild to moderate signs: thirst, dry mouth, lips and tongue, dizziness or light-headedness (especially when standing up), headache, dark-coloured urine, passing urine less often than usual.
- Severe signs: extreme thirst, fast breathing, fast heart rate, low blood pressure, irritability, tiredness or confusion, cold hands and feet, pale skin, sunken eyes, fever.
- You are more at risk with vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, too much alcohol, strenuous exercise in hot weather, some medicines, or diabetes.
- Prevent it by drinking enough fluids. Drink water even if you do not feel thirsty.
- If someone is confused, collapsing or very unwell in the heat, see the Heatstroke card and call 000.

items.title: Staying well in hot weather
items.text:
Heat-related illness can quickly become life threatening. If you or someone near you is very unwell and does not respond to cooling and rehydration quickly (within 10 minutes), call 000 and ask for an ambulance (healthdirect).
- Drink plenty of water, even if you are not thirsty.
- Stay out of the sun. Wear light-coloured, loose-fitting clothes. Wear sunscreen and a hat if you must go outside.
- Plan your day around the heat. Avoid being outdoors between 11am and 3pm, and avoid physical activity.
- Cool showers or baths help. Use fans or air conditioning if you can.
- A heatwave is when minimum and maximum temperatures are hotter than usual for 3 or more days in a row.
- People at higher risk include those over 65, babies and young children, people with long-term health conditions, people who work outdoors and people not used to the heat.

items.title: Never leave children or animals in a hot car
items.text:
Never leave babies, children or animals alone in a car, even if the air conditioner is on (healthdirect).
- If animals are outside, make sure they have water and plenty of shade.
- Check on older friends, neighbours or relatives during hot weather.

items.title: Sun protection
items.text:
Cancer Council's SunSmart message is Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide: slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat, seek shade and slide on wraparound sunglasses.
- South Australia suggests hats, sunscreen, sunglasses, long-sleeved shirts and loose fitting pants for outback trips.
- Avoid being outdoors between 11am and 3pm in hot weather (healthdirect).
- Apply insect repellent after sunscreen (healthdirect).

items.title: Water sources and washing
items.text:
Natural water is not a safe drinking supply. Treat it as a last resort, and protect it for animals and other people.
- Do not rely on waterholes, dams, bores, mills, tanks or troughs for drinking water (Royal Flying Doctor Service).
- The Northern Territory Emergency Service suggests packing water purifier tablets, and some salt or salt tablets.
- Do not use soap or detergents in or near waterholes, stock watering points or artesian springs (South Australia). The Royal Flying Doctor Service says soap or detergents should not be used in any natural water course or stock watering point.
- Do not camp within 500 metres of stock watering points in South Australian outback areas.
- Fill your bucket from a different spot each time in crocodile country, and do washing and food preparation well away from the water's edge (NT Government, Be Crocwise).

items.title: Snakes: avoiding bites
items.text:
Snakes are shy. Their first defence is to move away from danger, including people. People are most commonly bitten when they try to kill or handle a snake (ACT Government).
- Move away and let the snake go on its way. Never try to catch, handle or kill it.
- Snakes are protected by law in all Australian states and territories. It is illegal to kill them unless they threaten life (ACT Government).
- Stick to trails and make a bit of noise when you walk. Wear sturdy enclosed footwear and long pants when bushwalking (South Australia).
- Be alert in the bush, especially in the early morning when snakes are more likely to be sunning themselves. Avoid long grass. Do not put your hand into hollow logs or rock crevices (ACT Government).
- Keep pets well away from snakes. If you see a snake near camp, move pets and children away for an hour or until it moves on (ACT Government).
- Always assume a snake may be venomous, even a small one (South Australia).
- If someone is bitten, use the Snake bite card and call 000.

items.title: Crocodile country: camping and fishing
items.text:
Saltwater crocodiles live in both fresh and salt water in the Top End. Never take unnecessary risks in crocodile habitat (NT Government, Be Crocwise).
- Never approach, interfere with or feed crocodiles, even small ones.
- Camp at least 50 metres from the water's edge, and avoid areas where animals come down to drink.
- Do washing and food preparation well away from the water. Choose a different spot to fill your bucket each time.
- Do not leave fishing scraps or food waste around your campsite. Do not clean fish or dispose of carcasses in or near the water (NT Emergency Service).
- Fishing from a boat: keep arms and legs inside the boat. Use a net or gaff to retrieve fish. The smaller the boat, the greater the risk.
- Fishing from the bank: stand at least 5 metres back from the edge. Do not go into the water to retrieve snagged gear.
- In northern Queensland, be extra careful around water at night and during the breeding season (September to April), and never feed crocodiles because it is illegal and dangerous (Queensland Government).

items.title: Swimming and waterholes
items.text:
Water that looks inviting can be dangerous.
- In the Northern Territory, only swim where there are designated safe swimming signs (NT Emergency Service, Be Crocwise).
- In northern Queensland, swim only in designated safe swimming areas. Even if there is no warning sign there may still be crocodiles (Queensland Government).
- Never dive or jump into waterholes or rivers. Supervise children, especially near water.
- Stay well back from cliff edges and waterfalls.
- Obey all warning signs.

items.title: Marine stingers (northern Australia)
items.text:
Dangerous tropical marine stingers, including box jellyfish and Irukandji, are in tropical Queensland waters all year round. The risk is higher during stinger season, November to May (Queensland Government).
- Swim at patrolled beaches between the red-and-yellow flags, and obey safety signs. Do not enter the water when beaches are closed.
- Swim in stinger nets where provided. Consider a full-body lycra suit.
- Do not touch stingers washed up on the beach. They can still sting.
- If stung, call 000 and ask for an ambulance. While you wait, pour vinegar on the sting. Start CPR if the person stops breathing normally.
- Irukandji symptoms can take 20 to 40 minutes to develop. If in doubt, seek medical help.

items.title: Sharks and beach swimming
items.text:
Sharks live along the Queensland coast and also in estuaries, rivers, creeks, canals and streams (Queensland Government).
- Swim between the flags at patrolled beaches. If a shark is spotted, lifesavers will sound a siren or ring a bell, put up the red-and-white flag and tell you to leave the water immediately.
- Do not swim at dawn or dusk.
- Swim in clear water. Avoid murky water, busy anchorages, estuary mouths and canals.
- Do not throw food scraps or fish waste overboard, and do not swim where fish are being cleaned.
- Swim, surf, snorkel or dive with a buddy.

items.title: Blue-ringed octopus
items.text:
Blue-ringed octopuses live in tide pools and shallow reefs all around Australia and are among the world's most venomous animals (Queensland Government).
- Bites happen when people touch or stand on them. The bite may be painless, but the venom in the saliva can be fatal.
- If bitten, call 000 immediately and ask for an ambulance. While the ambulance is on its way, apply a pressure immobilisation bandage to the bite site.
- Start and continue CPR if the person stops breathing normally.

items.title: Dingoes on K'gari (Fraser Island)
items.text:
Dingoes are wild apex predators. Do not treat them like pets, and do not feed them (Queensland Parks). The rules below are for K'gari. Other places may have different rules.
- Keep children within arm's reach.
- Carry a safety stick (a hiking pole, umbrella or fishing rod will do) when walking outside fenced areas. Never use it to harm or provoke a dingo.
- Stay at least four car lengths (20 metres) away from dingoes.
- Keep rubbish in a locked, airtight container or in your car. Keep food, cooking, cleaning and fishing items locked up or in your car.
- Do not run. Do not walk or sit alone outside fenced areas.
- Do not feed or interact with dingoes. It is an offence to feed or make food available to a dingo on K'gari.
- Do not bring food or have picnics on the lake shore or beach.

items.title: Mosquitoes and insect repellent
items.text:
Mosquito bites cause an itchy, red, swollen lump. Some mosquitoes carry diseases. The best way to lower your chance of a bite is to cover up and use insect repellent (healthdirect).
- Wear loose-fitting, light-coloured clothes with long sleeves and pants, plus socks and shoes.
- Use repellent on exposed skin. The best repellents contain DEET, oil of lemon eucalyptus or picaridin. Use products approved by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority.
- Apply repellent after sunscreen. Do not apply it near your eyes, mouth or broken skin.
- An adult should apply repellent to children under 5. It is not advised for babies under 3 months. Cover prams and cots with mosquito nets.
- In the Northern Territory mosquitoes are active around sunset, and repellent with a DEET base is advisable (NT Emergency Service).
- NSW National Parks also warns of leeches and ticks, and links to NSW Health advice on mosquito bite prevention.

items.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip
items.text:
Queensland Transport lists these essentials to check before you go. Have the vehicle serviced before a remote journey (NSW National Parks).
- Tyres: good condition and the right pressure, including the spare.
- Fluid levels: brake, coolant, oil, clutch, automatic transmission, power steering and water.
- Lights: headlights, high beams, reverse, indicators and brake lights.
- Windscreen wipers, in case of wet weather.
- Battery, fan belt condition and tension.
- Coolant hoses: no leaks and in good condition.
- Tow bar and connections, if towing.
- Enough fuel for the journey.
- Consider roadside assistance through your state motoring organisation before you go (NSW National Parks).

items.title: Engine overheating
items.text:
If the temperature gauge rises or a warning light comes on, act straight away (RACQ).
- Pull over in a safe place as soon as you notice signs of overheating, and switch off the engine.
- Do not keep driving, even a very short distance. It can greatly increase the damage and repair cost.
- Never remove the radiator cap from a hot engine. You could be scalded.
- Do not refill a hot engine with cold water. It can cause major damage. Let the engine cool fully, which can take several hours.
- Just adding water will not fix the problem. The cause must be found and fixed, and damage may not show for days or months.
- Prevention: check coolant levels regularly, have any coolant loss repaired, and watch the temperature gauge in hot weather.
- RACQ and RACV are motoring clubs, not government agencies. This advice is general. Check your vehicle's owner manual.

items.title: Flat battery and jump starting
items.text:
Modern vehicles can usually be jump started, but it is a high-risk job and mistakes can be costly (NRMA).
- If you are in any doubt, call roadside assistance. NRMA says it is safest to leave it to an expert.
- Do not jump start a damaged battery. Signs include physical damage, a rotten egg smell, or failing to restart after only a very short rest.
- Closely follow your owner's handbook, because different cars have different procedures.
- Use only high-quality jumper leads with spike protection, or a jump start pack. Connect them the right way round and in the order the manufacturer describes.
- Heat can strain a battery. Have the battery tested before the summer season (RACV).
- NRMA is a motoring club, not a government agency.

items.title: Changing a flat tyre safely
items.text:
If a tyre blows out while driving, do not panic. Grip the steering wheel firmly, compensate for the pull to one side, and do not brake hard straight away (Queensland Transport).
- Slow down gradually and turn on hazard lights. Stop on flat, stable ground away from traffic. Avoid bends, soft ground and steep hills.
- On a busy road or freeway shoulder, changing a tyre yourself is extremely risky. Call roadside help instead (RACV).
- Handbrake on. Park (automatic) or first gear (manual). Engine off. Chock the wheels if you can. Passengers should stand well away from traffic.
- Loosen the wheel nuts slightly before jacking. Use the jack only at the jacking points in your owner's manual, on stable level ground.
- Never put any part of your body under a vehicle held up only by a jack.
- Fit the spare, tighten the nuts by hand, lower the vehicle, then fully tighten in a criss-cross pattern.
- Many spare tyres are space-savers with lower speed limits (often around 80 km/h) and limited distance. Check the sidewall or manual, and replace it as soon as you can.
- Check your spare tyre pressure regularly. RACV is a motoring club, not a government agency.

items.title: Breakdown on a highway or busy road
items.text:
It is dangerous to exit your vehicle on or near high-speed roads (Queensland Transport).
- Exit the highway if you can. If not, pull onto the shoulder or as far from traffic as possible.
- Turn on hazard lights (and parking lights at night). Turn your wheels away from traffic. If safe, pop the bonnet.
- If it is safe, exit through the passenger side and move behind a barrier or as far from traffic as possible. If it is not safe to exit, keep seat belts fastened.
- Call your roadside assistance provider. Queensland Transport also lists 13 19 40. Give your location.
- If you have no phone and cannot safely walk to one, stay with your car. Do not walk along highways and do not attempt repairs.
- Keep a high-visibility vest and a torch in the vehicle, keep your phone charged, and save roadside assistance contacts.
- In a remote area, the rule is different: stay with your vehicle. See the Broken down or lost card.

items.title: Spares, tools and recovery gear
items.text:
Remote tracks are hard on vehicles.
- Carry two spare tyres, check both are inflated, and always have a long-handled shovel and a strong jack (South Australia).
- Carry a tyre gauge, air pump, shovel, traction aids, first-aid kit, water, food, fuel and spares on all sand trips (Queensland Parks).
- Tow ropes and snatch straps should only be used by trained operators with appropriately safety-rated equipment (Queensland Parks).
- Try not to use trees for winching. If you have no other option, use tree protectors (Queensland Parks).
- Carry a fire extinguisher (NSW National Parks and Queensland Transport).
- Know how to use traction aids and recovery gear before you need them (Queensland Parks).

items.title: Driving a vehicle in extreme heat
items.text:
Hot weather puts extra strain on vehicles (RACV).
- Check coolant, engine oil, brake fluid and power steering fluid.
- Tyre pressure rises in the heat. Check tyre pressure before heading off and check tread depth.
- On very hot days the road surface can become soft and sticky, especially if recently sealed. Avoid potholes and cracks.
- Watch the temperature gauge. Carry jumper leads, a torch, a phone charger, and extra coolant if travelling long distances in extreme heat.
- Drivers of older vehicles should carry a litre of oil and check the oil level regularly.
- Heat brings dehydration and fatigue. Drink water and take regular breaks.

items.title: Loading your vehicle and roof racks
items.text:
A heavy load on top increases the chance of a roll-over (Royal Flying Doctor Service).
- Pack the heaviest items low in the vehicle. Do not over-pack roof racks, because it can make the vehicle overturn (Queensland Transport).
- Pack light. The lighter you travel, the lower your fuel use and the less wear on your vehicle (South Australia).
- Consider the load your vehicle is carrying when you reduce tyre pressure on sand. Top-heavy vehicles topple more easily (Queensland Parks).

items.title: Driving on unsealed roads
items.text:
Unsealed roads can be gravel, sand or dirt. These surfaces can make your tyres lose traction (Queensland Transport).
- Reduce speed and increase the distance between you and the vehicle in front.
- Dry weather makes roads dusty and limits visibility. Wet weather makes them muddy, slippery and boggy.
- Braking distances are longer on unsealed roads, and 4WD vehicles are more unstable than conventional vehicles. Driving a 4WD does not mean you will not get bogged (NT Emergency Service).
- South Australia suggests lowering tyre pressure (start with around 80 per cent of road pressure) and reducing speed on unsealed roads.
- Queensland Parks warns that reduced tyre pressure affects performance. Avoid sharp turns, sudden braking, high speeds and rough surfaces. Tyres have come off their rims in serious accidents. Check your manufacturer's tyre pressure recommendations and re-inflate before sealed roads.
- On country roads, slow down before the road edge. The edge may drop off or have loose stones (Queensland Transport).
- Wear seatbelts. In the Northern Territory the driver is responsible for all passengers wearing one.

items.title: Dust, glare and low visibility
items.text:
Dust on outback roads can hide the road ahead (NT Emergency Service).
- In dust, pull over, stop and wait for it to settle. Turn your lights on so other vehicles can see you (Queensland Transport).
- When driving west, the afternoon sun can affect your vision from about 4pm (Queensland Transport).
- Sunrise and sunset can also limit your vision (Queensland Transport).
- If visibility is poor, use headlights or fog lights, or pull over until conditions improve.

items.title: Road trains and heavy vehicles
items.text:
Road trains are large truck and trailer combinations more than 19 metres long. In the Northern Territory some have three trailers and reach about 50 metres. They need plenty of room.
- Only overtake a road train when it is safe and road markings allow it. In the Northern Territory, make sure you have at least 1 km of clear, straight road ahead.
- Before overtaking, stay back at the 2-second following distance. Watch for soft shoulders, guideposts and wildlife.
- When it is safe, indicate, accelerate and overtake quickly without exceeding the speed limit. Changing down a gear may give you enough power. Keep your speed up so the road train does not have to brake after you pass.
- Do not cut in front of heavy vehicles, tailgate them, or speed up when one overtakes you.
- If you cannot see a heavy vehicle's side mirrors, assume the driver cannot see you.
- Keep a 2-second gap behind a heavy vehicle, and double it in bad conditions.

items.title: Wildlife and stock on the road
items.text:
Native animals and livestock use outback roads, mostly at dawn, dusk and night. Livestock can be on the roadside at any time (NSW National Parks).
- Avoid driving at sunrise, sunset and during the night where you can (NSW National Parks).
- Watch for livestock and wildlife on or beside the road. Slow down, flash your lights and beep your horn if animals are at the edge about to cross (Queensland Transport).
- If cattle or sheep are on the road, slow down or stop until they have moved off.
- In the Northern Territory, be especially wary of road-wandering buffaloes at dawn and dusk.
- Watch for potholes, loose gravel and other obstructions.

items.title: 4WD before you go
items.text:
Queensland Parks lists this checklist for 4WD trips into remote areas.
- Be proficient in 4WD driving. If you are a novice, drive with an experienced four-wheel driver.
- Pack good recovery gear and make sure your vehicle is in good working order.
- Check manufacturer's tyre pressure recommendations for different terrain.
- Check which roads and tracks you are allowed to drive.
- Plan your trip thoroughly: calculate distances, check refuelling points and allow plenty of time. Get local advice where possible.
- Pack detailed paper maps. Always let someone know where you are going and when you expect to return.
- Take reliable communication equipment such as a satellite phone or UHF radio, and a PLB.
- Stay with your vehicle if you break down or become stranded.
- Queensland road rules apply even on beaches.

items.title: Driving on sand and beaches
items.text:
Sand driving can be difficult and dangerous, and all road rules still apply (Queensland Parks).
- Check with local councils or park offices for restrictions and permits before driving on beaches. Some areas need a vehicle access permit.
- Engage 4WD and use low gears. Keep up momentum and avoid sharp turns.
- Drive on the harder sand between the waterline and the high tide mark. Travel at low tide or within 2 hours either side.
- Reduce tyre pressure on soft sand, but keep within the manufacturer's specifications. Carry a gauge and pump and re-inflate before hard surfaces.
- Keep off dunes except at designated crossing points. Do not drive on the drift line.
- Watch for people, animals and landing aircraft. Park at an angle to the water, away from traffic.
- Do not drive tired or after drinking. Never sit outside a moving vehicle.
- Marine turtles nest on beaches from November to April. Drive slowly, keep to the wet sand and avoid driving over nests. Do not use bright lights between 6pm and 6am.
- In remote beach areas, travel with at least one other vehicle.

items.title: Getting bogged
items.text:
Carry a shovel and traction aids, and know how to use them (Queensland Parks).
- Try traction aids and digging first. Tow ropes and snatch straps should only be used by trained operators with appropriately safety-rated equipment.
- Rangers cannot assist with towing or snatch strap recovery, because of the safety risks. They may suggest local towing services.
- If you are stranded, stay with your vehicle. It is easier to find than a person on foot (NT Emergency Service, Queensland Parks).
- Avoid getting stuck. Creeks can rise suddenly, roadsides can be boggy, and fallen trees and washouts can block remote tracks.
- If the track is blocked, do not drive off the road or into roadside drains. Turn back or find another open track.

items.title: Closed roads, gates and looking after the country
items.text:
- Closed means closed. Never drive into areas that are closed or have locked gates (Queensland Parks).
- In South Australia, severe penalties apply for driving on closed roads and they are enforced.
- Be prepared to turn back for fallen trees and washouts. Stay on the track.
- Do not drive into parks during and after heavy rain. You could be cut off for days (Queensland Parks).
- Pastoral properties are private. If you go off-road, make sure it is a public access road or get permission. Leave gates as you found them: closed gates closed, open gates open (NT Emergency Service).
- Do not carry plant seeds, soil or pests in footwear, clothing, vehicles and gear (Queensland Parks).
- Fire trails: avoid them after rain, and report damage or fallen trees (NSW Rural Fire Service).

items.title: Rest areas and truck bays
items.text:
- Never park in truck parking bays. They are for trucks and road trains, which need room to manoeuvre and often run noisy refrigeration units (Royal Flying Doctor Service).
- Rest areas are provided for fatigue breaks. Use caravan parks or camping grounds for overnight stops.
- In NSW, rest areas are not designated caravan sites and you cannot stay overnight (Transport for NSW). Rules differ between states.

items.title: Caravan weights: know your numbers
items.text:
Towing a caravan adds significant weight to your vehicle. Before you tow, weigh your caravan and vehicle, and know these numbers (Transport for NSW).
- Aggregate trailer mass (ATM): the maximum loaded mass of the caravan.
- Gross trailer mass (GTM), and your tow ball weight.
- Your towing vehicle's maximum towing capacity, and its gross combination mass (GCM) if the manufacturer supplies it.
- The loaded mass of your caravan must not exceed any of: the rated capacity of the towbar and tow coupling; the vehicle's maximum towing capacity; the caravan's maximum loaded carrying capacity (ATM); the rated carrying capacity of the tyres. The combined mass of vehicle and caravan must not exceed the GCM, if the manufacturer supplies one.
- Use a weigh station to check. Non-compliance may affect your caravan insurance cover, and unsafe loading can lead to fines.
- Rules shown here are from NSW. Check with the roads authority of each state you will travel in.

items.title: Towing rules (NSW)
items.text:
These rules are from the NSW Government. Other states have their own rules, so check the relevant roads authority if you travel interstate.
- You must not tow more than one trailer at a time.
- No person may travel in a trailer or caravan you are towing.
- You must secure and cover your load and make sure it does not overhang.
- Learner drivers and learner and provisional motorcycle riders are not allowed to tow. P1 car licence holders can tow only small trailers.
- If your vehicle (GVM) or vehicle and trailer combination (GCM) is over 4.5 tonnes, you must not exceed 100 km/h, whatever the signed limit.
- The overall length of the vehicle and trailer combination, including its load, must not be more than 19 metres.
- In NSW, attach a "do not overtake turning vehicle" sign to your caravan if the combined length of vehicle and caravan is 7.5 metres or more (Transport for NSW).
- You can get a fine and demerit points for towing illegally.
items.source_name: NSW Government: Towing a trailer or caravan

extra_sources.source_name: Transport for NSW: Caravans

items.title: Brakes, safety chains and couplings
items.text:
Minimum standards from the NSW Government. Check the rules for the state you are in.
- Trailers up to 750 kg gross trailer mass need no brakes. From 751 to 2000 kg, an efficient braking system on both wheels of at least one axle. From 2001 to 4500 kg, brakes on all wheels.
- A trailer with a gross trailer mass over 2 tonnes must have an automatic breakaway system in case it detaches from the vehicle. Brakes must be operable from the driver's seat.
- Couplings must be strong enough for a fully loaded trailer and have a positive locking mechanism.
- Safety chains must comply with Australian Standards. A loaded trailer under 2500 kg needs at least one chain. Over 2500 kg needs two.
- Chains should be as short as practicable and connected to the towing vehicle. Cross them over if two are fitted, so the drawbar does not hit the ground if the coupling fails.
- The towbar should be marked with its maximum rated capacity. Do not exceed the rated capacity of the towbar and coupling.
items.source_name: NSW Government: Towing a trailer or caravan

items.title: Caravan sway: what to do
items.text:
Trailers can jerk the back of the vehicle around and cause sway (snaking). Crosswinds, passing heavy vehicles and uneven road surfaces can cause it (Transport for NSW).
- If a trailer starts to sway, do not apply the vehicle's brakes, except as an absolute last resort.
- If the trailer's brakes can be operated by themselves, apply them gently.
- Otherwise hold a steady speed, or accelerate slightly if possible, until the sway stops.
- Prevent sway: use the accelerator, brakes and steering smoothly and gently, especially in wet or slippery conditions.
- Keep heavy loads towards the centre of the caravan and low.
- Transport for NSW recommends a towing vehicle with an electronic trailer sway control feature.
items.source_name: NSW Government: Towing a trailer or caravan

extra_sources.source_name: Transport for NSW: Caravans

items.title: Loading a caravan
items.text:
Poor loading is a common cause of sway. These are NSW Government guidelines.
- Keep heavy loads towards the centre of the trailer, as low and close to the axle or axles as possible.
- Aim for about 60 per cent of the total weight forward of the centre of the axle or axles.
- As a general rule, about 5 to 10 per cent of the total mass of the trailer plus load should be supported by the vehicle through the coupling.
- The drawbar should be level or slightly nose down.
- Do not overload the trailer. Secure and contain the load.
- Use the Transport for NSW caravan safety checklist to check that the caravan is packed safely and that brakes, lights and connectors work.
items.source_name: NSW Government: Towing a trailer or caravan

extra_sources.source_name: Transport for NSW: Caravans

items.title: Driving tips when towing a caravan
items.text:
Towing is different from normal driving (Transport for NSW and NSW Government).
- Allow for the extra length and width when entering traffic or changing lanes. The trailer tends to cut in on corners and curves, so allow extra road space.
- Leave a longer stopping distance. The longer and heavier the caravan, the more you need. Allow even more in poor conditions.
- Slow down well before corners. Avoid sudden lane changes and changes of direction.
- Use a lower gear downhill to control the vehicle and reduce the risk of brake failure.
- When reversing, have someone watch the rear of the caravan from a safe location.
- Look further ahead than normal.
- Keep left unless overtaking, and do not hold up traffic unnecessarily.
- Plan fewer hours on the road each day and take more rest breaks.
items.source_name: Transport for NSW: Caravans

extra_sources.source_name: NSW Government: Towing a trailer or caravan

items.title: Caravan checks before and during a trip
items.text:
Check these before each towing trip (NSW Government).
- Vehicle and trailer are roadworthy.
- All tyres are properly inflated.
- Wheel bearings, suspension and brakes work properly.
- All lights work and safety chains are properly connected.
- Oil, water, brake fluid, battery and other service checks on the vehicle are done.
At regular intervals during the trip, check that:
- Couplings, all doors, hatches, covers and any load or equipment are still properly secured.
- Tyres are still properly inflated and not rubbing on suspension or bodywork.

items.title: Total Fire Bans: what is allowed
items.text:
These are the NSW Rural Fire Service rules. Each state has its own rules, so check the fire agency for the state you are in. On Total Fire Ban days, no fires can be lit in the open.
- During a Total Fire Ban you cannot light, maintain or use a fire in the open, or do any activity in the open that causes or is likely to cause a fire. Hot works such as welding, grinding or gas cutting are not to be done in the open.
- Barbeques or pizza ovens that burn solid fuel (wood, charcoal or heat beads) cannot be used outside.
- An electric barbeque may be used under the direct control of a responsible adult who is present at all times, with no combustible material within 2 metres.
- A gas barbeque may be used under the same conditions, with an immediate and continuous supply of water, and either within 20 metres of a permanent private dwelling or in a designated picnic area with an appliance approved by the Council, National Parks or State Forest.
- Fire permits are suspended on Total Fire Ban days.
- Total Fire Bans are declared when weather is very hot, dry and windy. These are usually days with an Extreme or Catastrophic fire danger rating.
- The Northern Territory Emergency Service suggests taking a gas barbeque in case of a total fire ban.
items.source_name: NSW Rural Fire Service: Total Fire Ban rules

items.title: Campfire safety
items.text:
Only light a campfire if fires are allowed where you are, and never on a Total Fire Ban day.
- Only light fires in designated fireplaces where you can. Campfires may not be permitted in all parks, so check before you go (NSW National Parks).
- Place fires and barbeques at least 2 metres from flammable materials, on an existing fire site or cleared area where the wind will blow flames away from tents (NSW Rural Fire Service).
- Keep fires attended by a responsible adult and keep a water supply ready.
- Do not cook or smoke in tents.
- Extinguish fires, candles and lanterns before bed. Completely extinguish all fires before you leave an area or go to sleep.
- Do not use campfires to burn rubbish. Fire does not destroy aluminium foil, and plastics release toxic gases (NSW National Parks).
- Bring your own firewood. Dead wood is habitat for native animals, so do not collect fallen timber (NSW National Parks, South Australia).
- In South Australia, check fire restrictions with the Country Fire Service. Some national parks do not allow wood fires.

items.title: Bushfire: before you travel
items.text:
Know the fire risk for the area you are travelling to and check conditions each day (NSW Rural Fire Service).
- Check the Fire Danger Rating. If conditions are bad, do not risk it.
- Set up a watch zone in the Fires Near Me app (NSW) or the Hazards Near Me app, and download the Emergency+ app. Apps only work with mobile reception.
- Check local weather, fires, floods and park closures before you go.
- Know what you will do if a fire starts. See the Bushfire while travelling card for what to do in your state.
- Listen to local radio, TV and news for updates.

items.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings
items.text:
Never drive through floodwater. It can be deeper and faster than it looks, and you cannot see what is under it.
- Turn around on flooded roads and find a safer way. Only travel if essential (NSW SES).
- It takes just 15 cm of flowing water to float a small car. Floodwater can hide potholes, debris and washed-away road surfaces (Victoria SES).
- In the Northern Territory, unless you are sure of the water depth, flow rate and any road damage, do not attempt to cross flooded bridges or causeways. Do not ignore signs (NT Emergency Service).
- Queensland Parks: "If it's flooded, forget it." Do not drive through floodwaters or fast flowing creeks.
- Creeks can rise suddenly, and you may be cut off for days after heavy rain (Queensland Parks).
- If driving conditions are dangerous, pull over safely on higher ground, away from trees. Tune in to ABC local radio for updates (Victoria SES).
- If you are trapped in your car by rising flash floods, call 000. This is a life-threatening situation (NSW SES). See the Flood card.
- Throw out food and drink, including water, that has been in contact with floodwater (NSW SES).

items.title: Australian Warning System levels
items.text:
The NSW SES issues flood warnings using the Australian Warning System. The three levels are:
- Advice: an incident has started. Stay up to date in case the situation changes.
- Watch and Act: conditions are changing and you need to start taking action now. Do not enter floodwater. Prepare to evacuate.
- Emergency Warning: the highest level. You may be in danger and need to take action immediately.
- Download the Hazards Near Me app and set your watch zones for floods and severe weather to get NSW SES warnings (NSW SES).
- An emergency alert may be sent to your phone (text or voice message). Apps and alerts need mobile reception.
items.source_name: NSW SES: During a flood

items.title: Getting SES help in floods and storms
items.text:
Call 132 500 for emergency assistance in floods, storms and tsunami. In a life-threatening emergency, call 000.
- 132 500 is the number given by the NSW SES, Victoria SES and the Northern Territory Emergency Service.
- The SES may not be able to reach you immediately. You may need to rely on yourself, family, friends or neighbours for a period (NSW SES).
- Leave early, before roads are closed. If you stay, it may be too dangerous to rescue you (NSW SES).
- Staying at your safe location helps responders. Going to see affected areas makes response and recovery harder (NSW SES).

items.title: Choosing and setting up a campsite
items.text:
Advice from NSW National Parks for camping in national parks and remote areas.
- Check signage on the ground to see where camping is permitted. If you booked a specific campsite, go to your reserved spot.
- Look up when you set up camp. Check there are no loose, dead or overhanging tree limbs.
- Campsites are often next to unfenced rivers, lakes and creeks. Take care. Camp above flood and tide debris, do not camp in dry creek beds or road drains, and always supervise children.
- To protect the land at remote camping areas, avoid low or poorly drained areas where soil or vegetation may be easily damaged. Look for higher ground or sandier soils.
- Check the weather forecast. You may not be able to reach or leave the campground in wet weather.
- In crocodile country, camp at least 50 metres from the water's edge (NT Government).
items.source_name: NSW National Parks: Camping safety

extra_sources.source_name: NT Government: Be Crocwise, Crocodiles and me

items.title: Camping in national parks: booking, water and first aid
items.text:
These points are from NSW National Parks. Other states have their own rules.
- You may need to book in advance. Wild or back country camping is permitted in some parks, and does not need a booking if the campground is not listed. Filling in a trip intention form is highly recommended.
- Drinking water is not available at most campgrounds. Check before you arrive, and always carry enough drinking water.
- Check park alerts and closures and the Hazards Near Me app before you go.
- Bring a first aid kit. Check your camping equipment works before you leave.
- Plan ahead to reduce animal bites, including leeches, ticks and mosquitoes.
- In NSW parks, camping is usually restricted to within the boundaries of a campground.
items.source_name: NSW National Parks: Camping safety

items.title: Camping on pastoral land (South Australia)
items.text:
If you are not in a national park, you are most likely travelling through a pastoral property. It is someone else's backyard (South Australia Landscape Board).
- On public access routes through pastoral land, camp within 100 metres of the track, at least 1 kilometre away from homesteads or other buildings, and at least 500 metres away from stock watering points.
- Only signposted public access routes on pastoral stations can be used without first asking the landholder. All other station tracks are private.
- Stay on the tracks. Camp only in designated areas or areas permitted by the land manager.
- In the Northern Territory, pastoral properties are also private. Get permission, and leave gates as you found them.
- These distances are South Australian rules. Check the rules for the state you are in.

items.title: Aboriginal land and sacred sites
items.text:
Entering Aboriginal land generally requires an access permit.
- If you plan to travel through Aboriginal land (other than on designated highways), you must obtain a permit. Tour leaders organise permits for their tours. It is the right of Traditional Owners to refuse entry permits (Royal Flying Doctor Service).
- Permit applications and general enquiries must be made in writing to the relevant Land Council in each state (Royal Flying Doctor Service).
- In the Northern Territory, permission to enter Arnhem Land must be obtained from the relevant Land Council (NT Emergency Service).
- Some places and objects hold special significance for Aboriginal people. Visitors are welcome but must show respect. Some sites are protected by law and there are penalties for trespassing.

items.title: Toilets, rubbish and waste
items.text:
Arid landscapes are fragile. Every wheel you take off the track has a lasting impact (South Australia Landscape Board).
- Use public toilet facilities where available. If there is none, dig a deep hole, burn any toilet paper and fill in the hole.
- Take your rubbish and waste cassettes to town facilities. Do not empty cassettes into public toilets.
- Do not use soap or detergents in or near waterholes, stock watering points or artesian springs.
- Carry your rubbish home. If others have left a mess, consider cleaning it up (Queensland Parks).

items.title: Pets and camping
items.text:
Dogs and cats cannot be taken into national parks in some places.
- The Northern Territory Emergency Service says dogs and cats are not permitted in Northern Territory national parks and reserves.
- The Royal Flying Doctor Service says dogs and cats cannot be taken into national parks.
- Rules vary by state and park. Check with the park manager before you travel.
- In hot weather, never leave animals alone in a car. Make sure outdoor animals have water and plenty of shade (healthdirect).

items.title: Unresponsive person: DRSABCD and CPR
items.text:
Someone is not responding and not breathing normally.
Call 000 first.
1. Danger: make sure the area is safe for you and the person. Do not put yourself or others at risk. Remove the danger or the person.
2. Response: loudly ask their name and squeeze their shoulders.
3. Send for help: if there is no response, call 000 and ask for an ambulance, or ask someone else to call. Do not leave the person.
4. Airway: check their mouth and nose are clear. If there is something there, roll them into the recovery position and remove any obvious blockage. Open the airway by gently tilting the head back and lifting the chin.
5. Breathing: look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds. If they are breathing normally, put them in the recovery position, stay with them and keep checking. If they are not breathing normally, start CPR.
6. CPR (adult or child over 1 year): 30 chest compressions, then 2 breaths, and repeat. Push on the lower half of the breastbone, with your arms straight, about one third of the chest depth, at about 100 to 120 compressions a minute.
7. If you cannot give breaths, keep doing compressions without stopping. Compressions alone may still save a life.
8. Defibrillator: if an AED is available, attach it and follow its voice prompts. Do not leave the person alone or stop compressions to fetch one.
9. Keep going until they recover, a health professional takes over, or you are too exhausted to continue.
Call 000 if: Always, if the person is unresponsive. Babies under 1 year need a different technique: tell the operator and follow their instructions.

items.title: Snake bite
items.text:
Any known or suspected snake bite. Treat every bite as life-threatening, even if the person seems well.
Call 000 first.
1. Get the person away from the snake. Do not try to catch or kill it.
2. Call 000 and ask for an ambulance.
3. Lie the person down, keep them still and calm.
4. If the bite is on an arm or leg, put a wide (10 to 15 cm) elastic roller bandage firmly over the bite as soon as possible.
5. Put a second roller bandage on, starting just above the fingers or toes and moving up the limb as far as you can reach. It should be tight: you should not be able to easily slide a finger under it.
6. Keep the limb still with a splint.
7. Write down the time of the bite and the time the bandage went on. If you can, mark the bite site on the bandage or skin with a pen, or take a photo.
8. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR (see the DRSABCD card).
9. Stay with the person until the ambulance arrives.
- Do not wash the bite area. Venom on the skin and clothes helps identify the snake.
- Do not use a tourniquet.
- Do not cut the wound or try to suck the venom out.
- Do not try to catch or kill the snake.
Call 000 if: Always.

items.title: Heatstroke (very hot, confused or collapsed)
items.text:
Someone is very hot and has confusion, strange behaviour, seizures or has collapsed. Skin may be hot, red and dry, with little or no sweating.
Call 000 first.
1. Call 000 and ask for an ambulance. Heatstroke is a life-threatening emergency.
2. Move the person to a cool or shady place. Loosen and remove extra clothing.
3. Start cooling them straight away. Best: put their whole body from the neck down in cold water for 15 minutes.
4. Or wet them with cold or cool water using a shower, hose, wet cloth or spray, and fan them continuously.
5. Put ice packs on the groin, armpits, cheeks, palms and soles of the feet.
6. Only give cool drinks if they are fully awake and can swallow.
7. If they stop breathing, start CPR (see the DRSABCD card).
- Do not give paracetamol, aspirin or ibuprofen. They do not lower body temperature in heatstroke.
Call 000 if: Always, if heatstroke is suspected.

items.title: Severe bleeding
items.text:
Bleeding that cannot be controlled with firm pressure, or signs of shock (pale, cold, clammy skin, fast weak pulse, faintness).
Call 000 first.
1. Call 000 early. Follow DRSABCD.
2. Wear gloves if you have them. Lie the person down and expose the wound.
3. Press firmly, directly and continuously on the wound with your hands until bleeding stops. The person or a bystander can do this.
4. When you have a pad or dressing, put it on or in the wound and keep pressing.
5. If an object is stuck in the wound, press on either side of it and pad around it before bandaging.
6. Once bleeding is controlled, bandage the pad firmly in place. Watch for new bleeding.
7. If bleeding on an arm or leg is not controlled, apply an arterial tourniquet if you have one and tighten it until the bleeding stops. Warn the person it will hurt.
8. If bleeding is not on a limb and not controlled, use a haemostatic dressing if you have one, with firm pressure.
9. Keep checking their consciousness, breathing and pulse.
- Do not give the person anything to eat or drink.
Call 000 if: Always, for severe or uncontrolled bleeding.

items.title: Burns and scalds
items.text:
Burns from fire, hot water or steam, hot objects, chemicals or electricity.
Call 000 first.
1. If clothing is on fire: stop the person moving, drop them to the ground, cover or wrap them in a blanket and roll them until the flames are out.
2. Remove the cause. Electrical burn: turn off the power if it is safe. Chemical burn: remove contaminated clothing and wash with water (you can keep going for up to 60 minutes). Dry chemicals: brush them off first.
3. As soon as possible, hold the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. It can still help for up to 3 hours after the burn.
4. Take off clothing and jewellery from the area, unless it is stuck to the burn.
5. Cover the burn with a light, loose, non-stick dressing. Plastic cling film is a good choice, but do not use it on the face.
6. Watch for signs of shock.
- Do not use ice.
- Do not put lotion, cream, ointment or fat on a burn.
- Do not remove anything stuck to the burn.
- Do not burst blisters.
Call 000 if: The burn is deep (even if it does not hurt), is on the face, hands or genitals, has white, brown or black patches, was caused by chemicals or electricity, or affects the airway or breathing. Also get medical help for any burn bigger than a 20 cent coin.

items.title: Spider bite
items.text:
Bitten by a spider. Funnel-web and other big black spiders are dangerous. Redbacks are painful but not life-threatening.
1. Funnel-web or any big black spider: call 000 and ask for an ambulance. Lie the person down and keep them still.
2. Funnel-web or big black spider: wrap a wide (10 to 15 cm) elastic roller bandage over the bite, then a second one over the whole limb from just above the fingers or toes upwards. Firm, but not cutting off circulation. Keep the limb still with a splint. Mark the bite site and write down the time.
3. Redback: wash the bite with soap and water and put a cold pack on it for 15 minutes. See a doctor if symptoms are bad, and go to an emergency department if the pain is very bad.
4. Other spiders: wash with soap and water and apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth (never directly on skin). See a doctor if it gets worse.
5. Severe allergic reaction (difficult or noisy breathing, swollen tongue, tight throat, collapse): call 000. Use an adrenaline autoinjector if one is available.
- Only use the pressure bandage for funnel-web or mouse spider bites, not for redback or other spiders.
Call 000 if: Funnel-web or other big black spider bite, difficulty breathing, collapse or confusion.

items.title: Broken down or lost in a remote area
items.text:
Your vehicle is bogged or has broken down, or you are lost, far from help.
1. Stay with your vehicle. It gives shade and shelter, and it is much easier for searchers to find than a person on foot, especially from the air.
2. Call for help if you can: 000 by satellite phone or mobile if you have coverage. If you carry a registered PLB or EPIRB, activate it.
3. Make your position easy to see from the air, for example by spelling a word in large letters on the ground.
4. Use the water and supplies you carry carefully. In hot, dry conditions, running short of water becomes life-threatening quickly.
5. Only leave the vehicle if you must. Leave a note that says the direction you are going, what supplies you have, and the date and time you left.
6. If you move, leave marks on the ground (such as rock piles or stick arrows) so trackers can follow you.
Call 000 if: Anyone is injured or in danger, or you cannot get back to safety.

items.title: Flood and flooded roads
items.text:
Water over a road or creek crossing, flash flooding, or rising water around you.
1. Never drive, walk, ride or play in floodwater. If it is flooded, forget it. Turn around and find another route, or wait.
2. Floodwater can be deeper and faster than it looks. It can take just 15 cm of flowing water to float a car.
3. Stay away from drains, culverts, creeks, causeways and low-lying areas.
4. If you are driving when flash flooding starts, avoid flooded roads and stop on the highest nearby ground, away from trees.
5. If you are trapped by rising water, get to the safest, highest place you can (this may be on the car roof or higher ground) and keep moving to stay above the water. Call 000. This is life-threatening.
6. For flood help that is not life-threatening, call the SES on 132 500.
- Do not drive through floodwater.
Call 000 if: You or someone else is trapped by floodwater or in danger.

items.title: Bushfire while travelling (car)
items.text:
You see smoke or flames ahead, or a fire is threatening the road. Sheltering in a car is a last resort. It is extremely dangerous.
Call 000 first.
1. If you see smoke or flames, turn around and drive away from the fire. Do not drive towards it. Do not try to outrun it.
2. Call 000 if your life is at risk. Say where you are. Check official warnings when you have signal.
3. Only if you cannot escape: park off the road in a clear spot, away from trees, scrub and long grass. If you can, park behind a wall or rock outcrop and face the front of the car towards the fire.
4. Turn on the hazard lights (most agencies also say headlights). Close all windows, doors and air vents. Stay in the car. Do not get out and run.
5. Get down below window level, for example in the footwell. Cover yourself with a woollen blanket. Drink water.
6. ENGINE AND AIR-CON: the agencies do not agree. Read your state's advice in the list below and follow it.
7. Stay down until the fire front has passed. Then get out carefully, because the car will be very hot. Move to ground that has already burnt, and check for spot fires.
- Do not drive into smoke or towards a fire. Smoke can make it very dark and hard to see, and roads may be blocked.
- Do not get out of the car while the fire front is passing.
Call 000 if: Your life is at risk, or once the fire front has passed if anyone is hurt.
- NSW: Turn the engine off. Also: headlights and hazard lights on, close windows and air vents, face the car towards the fire. Air-con is not mentioned separately.
- VIC: When the fire front is close: shut all vents, turn off the air-con and turn off the engine. CFA calls a stationary car in a clear area a last resort with a high risk of injury or death. Its Easy English guide says to turn the engine off when you park.
- SA: When the fire front is close: shut all vents, turn off the air-con and turn off the engine. Hazard lights on. Park off the roadway. CFS also says do not try to outrun a fire in a car.
- QLD: Leave the engine running. Headlights and hazards on, close all vents and windows. Air-con is not mentioned. After the front passes, check for burning fires and do not move the car until it is safe.
- WA: Turn the air-con and the engine off. Call 000. Headlights and hazard lights on, close windows, doors and vents. DFES warns that sheltering in a vehicle gives only a slightly higher chance of survival than being caught in the open.
- TAS: Run the air-con while you can. When the fire front is close, turn the engine off and close all vents. Hazard lights on. Park off the road. Be ready to get out as soon as the fire has passed. TFS's newer 2023 guide only lists a stationary car in a clear area as a last resort, with no steps.
- TAS: Air-con off. The engine may be left running so the headlights keep working and the battery does not go flat. This differs from the TFS advice above. Headlights and hazards on, close all windows, doors and vents.
- NT: Keep the engine running. Hazard lights on, close doors, windows and vents, lie on the floor and cover yourself with woollen or cotton fabric. Do not open the doors or windows until the fire front has passed. Air-con is not mentioned.
- ACT: No advice about the engine or sheltering in a car found. ESA's bushfire pages and Bushfire Survival Plan do not give in-car steps. They say leave early, and if you are caught in a fire, protect yourself from the heat. Check esa.act.gov.au and the nearby NSW RFS advice above.

items.title: What to tell the 000 operator
items.text:
Stay calm, speak slowly and clearly, and stay on the line.
1. A Telstra operator answers first. Say which service you need: police, fire or ambulance. If you need an interpreter, say your language.
2. Say exactly where to send help. Read out the coordinates from the My location panel, then the nearest town, state, road name or landmark. In remote areas, give nearby roads, landmarks and the property name. If you are driving, say which way you are heading and the last town you passed. The operator will ask for the town and state you are calling from.
3. Say what has happened.
4. Say how many people are hurt, and whether they are awake and breathing.
5. Follow the operator's instructions and do not hang up until told to.
6. If it is not safe to speak, or you cannot speak, stay on the line. When the recorded message asks you to press 55, do that and you will be put through to police.
If there is no mobile coverage on any network, you cannot reach Triple Zero from a mobile phone. Your call can use any available mobile network, but not if none has coverage. Calls to 000 can also be made from a satellite phone. If you carry a registered PLB or EPIRB, use it. You cannot contact Triple Zero by SMS.

items.title: Ambulance costs
items.text: Calling 000 is free, but an ambulance is not always free. Medicare does not cover ambulance services, so you can be sent an invoice. Queensland and Tasmanian residents are generally covered by their state. Visitors to Queensland and Tasmania from other states are invoiced, and Tasmanians are not covered everywhere when interstate. South Australia says its ambulance service is not free or covered by Medicare. Check your ambulance cover or travel insurance before you travel. Costs and rules differ by state and change over time, so check the state ambulance service.
